data.headline: Stock 2 weeks extra now, raise price 2% in week 8
data.why: The plan beats steady rivalry by $2,786 and weathers a cocoa shock with a $2,767 gain. Extra stock covers the 3-week lead time. A modest 2% rise in week 8 keeps the 55% loyal base while matching the rival's $18.36 level. Payback arrives week 5, peak cash $5,949, well inside the $8,640 buffer.
data.watch_out: If cocoa futures reverse their recent drop and surge past the June $8,402 peak, unit cost could jump 35% and erase the margin. The bad case is a 10% US tariff spreading to EU imports, lifting landed cost further.
data.recheck_when: Recheck at week 8 price move or if cocoa futures break above $8,200/tonne.

what_happened.text: Cocoa fell to a 20-month low near $6,090 a tonne as demand weakened and better West African harvests were expected.
European cocoa grindings, a measure of demand, were reported at their weakest fourth quarter in years, and prices kept falling.
The World Bank's monthly cocoa price was $3.24 a kg, down from $7.03 in September 2025.

caveats: Cocoa is set at 35% of a box's cost. A 2026 industry note puts cocoa at about 60% of a mass-market milk bar's raw materials (natriumcapital.com); a praline box has more labour and packaging, so we took a lower share. It is our estimate.
Prices in euros are converted at €1 = $1.08, the app's fixed rate. Couverture is priced off cocoa beans and butter with a lag, and many shops buy forward, so the shop did not pay the spot price.
This case's date is close to Nemotron Ultra's stated pre-training cutoff (September 2025), so it may not know what followed, unlike the 2022-2024 cases.
Each monthly value is treated as the month's mid-point, with straight lines between them.

The model has seen this period. Nemotron Ultra's model card gives a pre-training cutoff of September 2025 and a post-training cutoff of May 2026, so a date in the prompt cannot make it forget. The run only gives it news from before the date, and the leak check looks for hindsight in what it wrote.

“Best plan in hindsight” is the best of about 230 plans on a fixed grid (price, start, end, extra stock), run on the real path. Shoppers react to a sweep plan like they did to the nearest price plan the analysis tested; with none tested, they are neutral.
News pages are read as they are today. Any article that names a date after the as-of date is dropped, but a page edited later could still carry hindsight.

A plan that switches supplier is scored with the share of the price rise that Ultra assumed the alternative supplier would feel (`alt_shock_exposure`). The real price path says nothing about whether another supplier would really have been shielded, so those plans' results rest on that assumption.
